pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** States of Matter Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE, formal home Y4 'States of matter'; introduced informally earlier):** England's statutory treatment sits in Year 4 — "compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases." The non-statutory guidance supplies the child-friendly descriptors this vocabulary node teaches: "solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container," and pupils "observe water as a solid, a liquid and a gas." At ages 5–7 there is no KS1 statutory states content, so this is early, informal vocabulary-building that seeds the Y4 objective.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states; the nearest is DCI PS1.A ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]', anchoring 2-PS1-1) and 2-PS1-4 on reversible/irreversible heating/cooling changes. State-naming is treated as embedded vocabulary rather than a discrete PE.

- **Operational details:** Build the three category words from OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR, not definitions: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (forms a pool not a pile), a gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Use water as the anchor substance seen in all three states (ice, water, steam/vapour) so the SAME material carries the vocabulary. Introduce 'change of state' as the word for what happens when ice melts or water boils. Sort plentiful everyday examples and talk through borderline cases (is sand a solid? is it still a solid when it 'pours'?). Deliberately name a gas children can feel but not see (air in a balloon) to start dislodging 'gas isn't really stuff'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can correctly sort everyday substances as solid, liquid or gas and give a behaviour reason for each, use the three words accurately in description, and use 'change of state' to describe ice melting or water boiling.
bestPractices: Define each state by observable behaviour ('keeps its shape' / 'forms a pool not a pile' / 'fills its container'), not abstract definitions.
Use water as the through-line — ice, water, steam — so one familiar material demonstrates all three states and the change-of-state word.
Sort many real examples and talk through tricky cases (sand, powder, honey) to test the behaviour rule rather than surface looks.
Introduce a felt-but-unseen gas (air in a balloon, bubbles) early to begin challenging 'gas is not stuff'.
Handle everyday 'gas' language carefully — clarify the science sense versus natural gas/petrol so the word doesn't mislead.
Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water) at this age; avoid heating that causes burning/cooking (a chemical change).
keyRepresentations: Water shown in three states (ice cube, glass of water, steam) as the anchor example
Behaviour cards: 'keeps its shape' / 'flows, takes the shape of its container' / 'spreads to fill the space'
A three-bin sort (solid / liquid / gas) of everyday substances
A balloon or bubbles to make an invisible gas tangible
A simple melt/boil before-after pair introducing 'change of state'
commonMisconceptions: Gases are not matter / are weightless — rooted in 'seeing is believing' since most gases are invisible (a very common and persistent idea).
A 'solid' must be hard and rigid, so powders and sand (which pour) get miscalled liquids.
Thinking of a liquid as anything that pours, conflating flow with the liquid state.
The everyday meaning of 'gas' (fuel) crowding out the physical-state meaning.
Treating steam/water vapour as something other than water, or as 'hot air', rather than water in its gas state.

learn.summary: Early (ages 5–7) informal vocabulary-building for the three states of matter — solid, liquid, gas — anchored to OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR rather than abstract definitions: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (forms a pool not a pile), a gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Water is the through-line (ice, water, steam) so one familiar material carries all three words plus 'change of state'. It deliberately makes an invisible gas tangible (air in a balloon) to begin unseating 'gas is not stuff'. This seeds the later UK Year 4 objective; at this age there is no KS1 statutory states content, and NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states. (Steam, meaning water vapour, is the gas state and is invisible; the white cloud seen above a kettle is tiny drops of liquid water that form as the steam cools, so it should not be presented as the gas.)

activities.title: Tap-to-name the three states in a kitchen scene
feedback: When a learner taps an item, state the name AND the behaviour reason together ('LIQUID — it flows and takes the shape of the cup'), so the word is always tied to behaviour rather than appearance.

On the balloon, reinforce that the air spreads to fill the balloon and takes up space — a gas is a real material, not 'nothing'. (You can also feel it is really there by gently squeezing a sealed balloon, but the key point is that a gas fills and takes up space, not that it 'pushes'.)
On the water trio, name that ice, water and steam are all the same water in different states.
activities.rationale: This is a language node: attaching three category words to observable behaviours for early, pre-reading learners suits tap-to-reveal with audio and picture support (no reading required). Using water as one anchor material lets all three words and 'change of state' hang on something already known, consistent with the curriculum descriptors. Optional details such as lift-the-flap melting/boiling and a tappable balloon make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory descriptors 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'; observe water as solid, liquid, gas.
learnerActions: Explore a home/kitchen scene and tap everyday items to hear each one's state and the behaviour reason, e.g. tap the ice cube → 'SOLID — it keeps its shape'; tap the juice → 'LIQUID — it flows and takes the shape of the cup'; tap the kettle → 'When water boils it becomes steam, a GAS you can't see — it spreads out into the air. The white cloud is tiny water drops made as the steam cools.'

Visit a dedicated water trio panel showing the SAME water as hard ice, runny liquid, and invisible steam (water vapour) shown as spreading arrows or a dotted cue, with audio explaining that you can't see the gas itself.
Open a 'melting' and a 'boiling' flap on the water panel to hear that the move between states is called a 'change of state'.
Tap the balloon in the corner to hear 'the air inside is a GAS — it fills the balloon up'.
activities.intendedInsight: Three new category words attach to familiar things through how they behave (shape and container), and the SAME water can be solid, liquid or gas (the gas, steam or water vapour, is invisible), with 'change of state' naming the move between them; a gas (air) really is stuff that spreads out to fill its container.

activities.title: Sort real substances into solid / liquid / gas bins
feedback: For sand/sugar/salt placed as liquid: zoom in on a single grain — it is a hard solid that keeps its shape; the PILE pours only because the grains slide past each other.
For a damp sponge called 'a liquid': re-anchor to behaviour — the sponge keeps its shape (solid) even though it is wet.
When an item behaves as sorted, confirm using the behaviour phrase ('yes — it spreads to fill the jar, so it's a gas').
activities.rationale: Sorting many real examples and talking through tricky cases tests the behaviour rule rather than appearance, and the self-checking 'watch it behave' actions make the defining behaviours observable. Repeated hands-on sorting is reported to support conceptual change at this age. This does slightly more than a bare naming task, which is appropriate for the borderline cases. A sort of this kind can teach and check classification but does not by itself elicit the child's spoken explanation, so the checkpoint below adds spoken use.
sourceClaims: Elementary states-of-matter misconceptions are partly developmental; steam/water vapour confused with 'hot air'; powders/solids confusion; hands-on repeated activities needed for conceptual change.
learnerActions: Drag or place plentiful everyday substances into three bins labelled solid, liquid and gas.

For a chosen item, trigger a short 'watch it behave' action — a liquid pouring and taking the shape of a cup, a solid holding its shape, a gas (shown with a coloured animation cue, since most gases are invisible) spreading to fill a jar — and check the sort against the behaviour.
Discuss borderline cases out loud: Is sand a solid when it 'pours'? What about honey, sugar, salt, or a damp sponge?
Use a mini melt/boil before-after pair to practise the words 'change of state'.
activities.intendedInsight: The defining test is BEHAVIOUR (keeps its shape / flows and takes its container's shape / spreads to fill the space), not surface looks, size, smell or wetness; tricky cases like pourable powders are still solids because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Use the words like a scientist (checkpoint)
feedback: Expected: rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours).
'Change of state' = the same material in a different state, e.g. ice (solid) melting to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezing back.

If the learner says the balloon has 'nothing' or 'just air': make the gas tangible as a demonstration — squeeze the sealed balloon or fan the air onto a face so it can be felt; this shows the gas is really there and takes up space, filling its container (the 'push' you feel is the trapped air, not the definition — the point is a gas is a real material that fills the space).
If 'solid' is taken to mean strong/big, 'gas' only petrol/fumes, or 'liquid' any wet thing: re-anchor each word to BEHAVIOUR (shape and container), not size, smell or wetness.
Listen for the words used correctly in context ('fills its container', 'keeps its shape'), not merely recited; naming the trio alone (recitation) is not enough.
activities.rationale: The sand and air cases discriminate meaningful use from recitation: sand pours yet is solid, and gas is invisible yet real. Listening for USE exposes loose everyday usage a definition would hide. Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water); avoid heating that causes burning/cooking, which is a different kind of change. The misconception that a gas is 'not matter' is well attested, which is why the air case is included (source verification status noted in reviewNotes).
sourceClaims: 'Gas has no mass / gas is not matter' is a common, persistent misconception rooted in the 'seeing is believing' principle because most gases are invisible; everyday 'gas' language and 'empty' containers reinforce it.
learnerActions: Name whether each of several things is solid, liquid or gas AND describe HOW it behaves: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.
Explain what 'change of state' means, using ice as the example (ice melting to water, or water freezing back), including what happens to ice on a warm day.

Answer probing questions: Is the air in the balloon solid, liquid or gas — how can you tell it's really there? Sand pours like a drink — is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain. Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid — what makes it hard to decide?
activities.intendedInsight: Correct, meaningful USE of the behaviour-vocabulary in context (including tricky cases) shows genuine understanding, not recitation of the three words.

constraints: Define each state by observable behaviour ('keeps its shape' / 'forms a pool not a pile' / 'fills its container'), not abstract definitions.
Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water) at this age; avoid heating that causes burning or cooking, which is a different (chemical) kind of change.
Handle everyday 'gas' language carefully — distinguish the science sense (a state of matter) from natural gas/petrol/fumes so the word doesn't mislead.

All materials should be picture + audio with no reading required for ages 5–7; recognition/sorting and tap-to-reveal are supportive scaffolds that can teach and check classification, but they do not by themselves elicit the child's spoken use, so the checkpoint requires the child to USE the words aloud in context.

A linear quiz (categorization, matching, picture multi-select) can assess and score the vocabulary and may be used during teaching with heavy audio support, but it checks recall rather than building the behaviour-based categories; it is a supporting scaffold, not the core activity.

A tactile real-world version (handling real ice/water, real sand, a real balloon) and a screen scene offer different experiences; where safe, real substances can strengthen behaviour-based reasoning. Use adult supervision for any boiling/steam.

The 'air can be felt' balloon demonstration shows a gas is really there and takes up space; present it as a hands-on demo, not as a formal pressure explanation, and do not define a gas as 'something that pushes'.

Present steam (water vapour) as the gas state: it is invisible and spreads out into the air, and it is the same water as the ice and liquid. Do not call the visible white cloud above a kettle a gas; at this age simply say it is tiny water drops made when the steam cools.

This is early, informal vocabulary-building: at ages 5–7 there is no KS1 statutory states content, and NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states (nearest is PS1.A observable-property classification and 2-PS1-4 on reversible/irreversible heating/cooling). State-naming is embedded vocabulary, not a discrete standard.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: no arithmetic claims present. The 'sand pours but is solid' and 'air in a balloon is a gas' reasoning is internally consistent; the single-grain explanation and tangible-balloon demonstration are retained as the key discriminators.

The claim that air 'pushes back' / a gas 'can be felt to resist' is a pressure effect for a sealed/inflated balloon, not a general definition of a gas; it is framed only as a tangible demonstration that a gas is really there and takes up space, and the definitional language is 'spreads to fill / takes up space' in every learner-facing item.

One source (Victorian DoE Science Continuum / RSC Beyond Appearances) is marked verified:false in the row; the misconception it supports is widely attested, but its verification status is unconfirmed here and no fresh verification was performed.

Visible 'steam' is partly condensed water droplets, not pure water vapour; treating it as the gas state is an age-appropriate simplification carried over from the original and flagged as an approximation rather than re-verified.

The original row rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor' with comparative/necessity claims ('adds no naming power', '3D adds nothing'); these are not established by catalog ratings and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken use of the vocabulary is instead retained within the checkpoint as a narrow objective (recognition alone does not elicit production).
Minor concrete detail: the original's 'bubbles' example was collapsed into the balloon demonstration; it could be restored as an additional felt-but-unseen gas example.

probeDeeper: Is the air in this balloon a solid, liquid or gas — and how can you tell it's really there?
Sand pours like a drink — so is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain.
Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid? What makes it hard to decide?
Say what happens to ice on a warm day using the words 'change of state'.
assess.correctAnswer: Rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours). 'Change of state' = when ice (solid) melts to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezes back — the same material in a different state.

errorPatterns.pattern: Air/gas is 'nothing' — won't call the air in the balloon a gas or a material; treats gas as empty space.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make gas tangible: squeeze the sealed balloon, fan the air onto a face, feel it resist — a gas fills its container and can be felt, so it is a real material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the balloon has 'nothing' or 'just air' rather than a gas that fills it and pushes back.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Sand is a liquid because it pours' — uses flows/liquid for a pourable solid.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom on a single grain: it is a hard solid that keeps its shape; the PILE pours only because the grains slide past each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies sand (or sugar, salt) as a liquid because the pile pours.

errorPatterns.pattern: Everyday clash — 'solid' taken to mean strong/big, 'gas' only petrol or smelly fumes, 'liquid' any wet thing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word to BEHAVIOUR (shape and container), not to size, smell or wetness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a heavy object 'more solid'; reserves 'gas' for fumes; calls a damp sponge 'a liquid'.

responseLevels.gap: Uses solid/liquid/gas loosely by size or wetness; denies air is a gas; cannot use the behaviour-words.
responseLevels.full: Uses the state names and behaviour-vocabulary (keeps its shape / flows / fills its container) correctly in context including tricky cases, and uses 'change of state' accurately for melting and freezing.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three states for clear cases and uses some behaviour-words, but slips on tricky cases (sand as liquid, gas as 'nothing').

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'I'll name some things and I want you to tell me, like a scientist, whether each is a solid, a liquid or a gas — and describe HOW it behaves using proper words: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.' Then: 'Now tell me what “change of state” means, using ice as your example.' Listen for the words used correctly, not recited.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sand and air cases test whether the child uses the behaviour-words meaningfully rather than reciting the trio: sand pours yet is solid, and gas is invisible yet real. Listening for USE ('fills its container', 'keeps its shape') exposes loose everyday usage a definition would hide.
